title: Assignment Hidden Inside an If Condition

options.text: Compilation error because assignment cannot appear inside an `if` condition

explanation: `x = 0` is an assignment, not a comparison. It assigns 0 to `x`, and the resulting value 0 is converted to `false`. The first branch is skipped. Because `x` is now 0, `x == 7` is also false, so the final `else` executes and prints `C`.

title: The Dangling Else Trap
explanation: The first `else` belongs to the nearest unmatched `if`, which is `if (y > 5)`. Since `x > 5` is true, the nested `if` is reached. `y > 5` is false, so its `else` executes and prints `B`.

title: Impossible Chained Comparison

options.text: `Valid`, because the expression is evaluated as `(0 < x) < 10`
Compilation error because C++ prohibits chained comparisons
Undefined behavior because the comparisons conflict

explanation: C++ evaluates the comparisons from left to right here. `0 < 50` produces `true`, which behaves numerically as 1. The remaining comparison becomes `1 < 10`, which is true. Therefore `Valid` is printed. The intended test should be `x > 0 && x < 10`.

title: Semicolon That Silently Breaks an If Statement

options.text: Compilation error because the `else` has no matching `if`

explanation: The semicolon immediately after the `if` forms the complete body of that `if` as an empty statement. The following `cout << "Pass";` is a separate statement. Therefore the subsequent `else` has no unmatched `if` to which it can attach, causing a compilation error.

title: Switch Fall-Through Prediction
explanation: Execution jumps directly to `case 2`, so `A` is not printed. `B` is printed, but there is no `break`, so execution falls through into `case 3`, which prints `C`. The `break` then exits the switch. The output is `BC`.

title: Duplicate Switch Cases Hidden by Constant Expressions

options.text: Compilation error because both case labels represent the same constant value
Runtime error because C++ cannot evaluate arithmetic in a case label

explanation: `2 + 2` is a constant expression whose value is 4. Therefore `case 2 + 2:` and `case 4:` are duplicate case values. A switch cannot contain duplicate case values, so the program fails to compile.

title: Ternary Operator and Integer Division

options.text: Compilation error because the ternary branches have integer operands

explanation: Since `a > b` is true, only `a / b` is selected. Both operands are integers, so `7 / 2` performs integer division and produces 3. That integer is then converted to `double` when assigned to `result`, giving `3.0`; with default `cout` formatting it prints `3`.

title: Comparison Assignment and Ternary Precedence
explanation: The conditional operator is right-associative, so the expression is interpreted as `x > y ? x : (y == 8 ? 20 : 30)`. Since `5 > 8` is false, the second ternary expression is evaluated. `y == 8` is true, so `z` becomes 20.

title: Else-If Boundary Logic Error

options.text: There is no bug; a score of 90 prints `A`
A score of 90 falls through both conditions and incorrectly prints `C`
A score of 90 satisfies both conditions, producing ambiguous output
The program does not compile because `&&` cannot combine comparisons

explanation: For `score = 90`, the first condition `score > 90` is false, and the second condition requires `score < 90`, which is also false. Therefore the final `else` executes and incorrectly prints `C`. The first condition should include 90, such as `score >= 90 && score <= 100`.

title: Nested Selection with Short-Circuit Evaluation

options.text: Runtime error caused by division by zero

explanation: In the first condition, `x != 0` is false, so `&&` short-circuits and `y / x` is never evaluated; therefore there is no division by zero. In the `else if`, `x == 0` is true, so `||` short-circuits and `++y` is not evaluated. Thus `y` remains 4 and the program prints `4`.
